title: Do people keep right in a two-way corridor, and which robot passing policy keeps their lanes?
lede: research programme: do people keep right in a two-way corridor, and what do robots do to their lanes? In the Jülich HERMES experiments (24 runs, 4,752 walkers) people with no exit instruction walked on their own right 93.7% of the time (95% CI 0.865 to 0.993) in near-perfect two-lane flow, and assigning each a left or right exit cut that to 0.53 while lanes weakened; next, crowd models fitted to these runs and robots added
summary: An open research programme on which passing policy a fleet of mobile robots should use in a corridor shared with people, with the crowd models fitted to real trajectories and cross-checked across model families (social force, ORCA, the anticipatory power law). Milestone 1 measures the human baseline in the Forschungszentrum Jülich HERMES bidirectional corridor experiments (2009; 24 runs; 4,752 walkers tracked at 16 fps; DOIs 10.34735/ped.2009.10–12). With no instruction about the exit, 1,016 of 1,084 walkers (0.937, two-stage bootstrap 0.865 to 0.993) walked on their own right, both streams on the same relative side, and lane order was 0.91 to 1.00 against 0.25 to 0.52 for shuffled directions. When each walker was told to leave by the left or right exit, the share fell to 0.534 (0.503 to 0.568) over 13 symmetric runs and 0.526 over the asymmetric set, and lanes persisted at lower order (0.59 to 0.85, above the null in every run). Three of five registered predictions held; the share did fall at the highest density (0.82) and the free-speed run walked at 1.73 m/s, above the predicted range. Limits: ‘right’ assumes the archive frame is right-handed with z up; instruction is confounded with run order and corridor width, so the collapse is descriptive until the BaSiGo 2013 replication; laboratory crowd of students; no robots yet.
